newsitem.title: USA: U.S. chip industry barometer seen flat to higher.
newsitem.headline: U.S. chip industry barometer seen flat to higher.

text.p: The semiconductor industry's key barometer is expected to be flat to slightly higher for November, reflecting a continued rebound in demand for computer chips.

According to a Reuter survey of analysts, the November book-to-bill ratio, which measures the value of orders to sales, is expected to range from 1.10 to 1.12. The ratio rose to 1.10 in October, its first reading above break-even this year, the Semiconductor Industry Association reported.
The report is tentatively scheduled for release after the market close today, but delays in compiling the data could postpone the release until Tuesday.

A ratio of 1.12 would mean that chip makers received $112 worth of orders for every $100 in chips they sold last month. An index above 1.00 means the industry is expanding while an index below 1.00 means it is contracting.
Industry analysts said the recent strength in chip orders should keep the ratio flat to slightly higher against the October reading.
"I think it will be up about two basis points from whatever the revised October number is," Schroder, Wertheim analyst Stuart Johnson said. "Things are reasonably strong."
Bear Stearns analyst Nimal Vallipuram predicts a ratio of 1.10 will be reported.
Johnson said November was not likely much stronger than October. But the ratio is calculated as a three-month moving average, and August was much stronger than July.
The November ratio will be stronger because it no longer has July data in its averaging, he said.
Overall, the U.S. chip industry has been experiencing a rebound this autumn from most of 1996. The book-to-bill ratio was negative, or below 1.0, until October and hit a low point of 0.79 in March.
Analysts say business is good now and the ratio and its underlying orders and sales volumes should continue to get stronger in the months ahead.
Dan Niles of Robertson, Stephens & Co predicts a November ratio of 1.11.
Though historically widely watched on Wall Street, the book-to-bill ratio is losing its clout and will be replaced by a worldwide report in January.
Niles said "it doesn't matter anymore" what the book-to-bill ratio is because of the upcoming change.
